sections.title: The Parameters of the Prohibitions of Closeness
sections.html:
Throughout the time a woman is impure as a nidda (a menstruant), that is, from the time she saw blood until she immerses for her purification, she and her husband are forbidden to have marital relations, as it is stated (Vayikra 18:19): “Do not come near a woman during her period of impurity to uncover her nakedness.” It is also stated (ibid. 20:18): “If a man lies with a woman in her infirmity and uncovers her nakedness, he has laid bare her source and she has exposed the source of her blood; both of them shall be cut off from among their people.”

Not only is the union itself forbidden, but also any touch of desire that leads toward union, such as embracing and kissing, is forbidden; and even touching with the little finger for the sake of such desire is forbidden, as it is stated (ibid. 18:19): “Do not come near a woman during her period of impurity to uncover her nakedness.” According to most authorities, the meaning is that any touch involving the pleasure of desire is forbidden by Torah law (Rambam, Ra'avad and Ḥinukh). And the Sages made a safeguard for the mitzvot and forbade even touch that involves no pleasure or desire, and forbade this even through clothing. Some say that only the union itself is forbidden by Torah law, and touch without union is forbidden rabbinically (Ramban).1

As we will learn later in the chapter, the Sages went further and set additional safeguards, through whose observance the couple will succeed in overcoming their inclination during the days of prohibition; as a result their love will be refined and become deeper and more faithful, and in the days of purity they will merit to rejoice in the mitzva of ona (marital relations) with extra joy.

It is related in the Talmud (Sanhedrin 37a) that a Christian priest asked Rav Kahana: You say that a man is permitted to be in a closed house with his wife when she is a nidda. “Is it possible for fire to be in flax and not singe it?!” That is, is it possible that a couple who long for each other will overcome their inclination and not sin? He answered him: “The Torah testified about us: ‘hedged about with roses’ (Shir Ha-shirim 7:3) – that even with a hedge (fence) of roses, they do not break through it.” That is, Israel has a wonderful trait: by observing safeguards as soft as roses, without police to enforce the observance of the mitzvot, they succeed in overcoming their inclination and refraining from transgression. And this is one of the roles of the Sages, to set safeguards for the Torah, so that the Torah will be upheld in Israel, as it is stated (Vayikra 18:30): “You shall keep My charge,” that is, make a protection and safeguard for the mitzvot of the Torah (Avot 1:1; Mo'ed Katan 5a; Yevamot 21a). And Israel is commanded to observe the enactments of the Sages, as it is stated (Devarim 17:11): “You shall act in accordance with the instructions they give you and the ruling they hand down to you; you must not deviate from the word that they tell you, either to the right or to the left.”

sections.title: Conduct During the Days of Prohibition
sections.html:
As a safeguard for the prohibition, during the days of prohibition one must avoid conversations about matters connected with the joy of union and things that arouse toward it. This is what the Torah meant in its warning: “Do not come near a woman during her period of impurity” – that he should not embrace and kiss his wife, and also not “speak idle words with her” (Avot De-Rabbi Natan 2). That is, although in the days of purity talk connected with the joy of union is part of the mitzva of ona, during these days it is forbidden and is therefore considered idle words.

In addition, during the days of prohibition one must be careful not to converse at length about various matters that are liable to arouse their desire, each couple according to what they know from their own experience. According to many, this is what the Sages meant in their warning: “Do not converse much with a woman; they said this regarding one's own wife [when she is a nidda], all the more so regarding another man's wife” (Avot 1:5, according to the interpretation of Or Zarua 1:360; Rokeaḥ, Ha-manhig, Melekhet Shlomo and others). Included in this, during these days one should avoid a couple's holiday, which by its nature arouses extra closeness.

In a similar vein we learn from the words of the Sages (Shabbat 64b), who deliberated over whether it is right for a woman to wear make-up and adorn herself during the days of prohibition. The early elders expounded: “And she who is ill in her impurity (nidatah)” (Vayikra 15:33) – nidatah is a term of banishment and distance; therefore “she should not paint (her eyes), nor rouge (make up her face), nor adorn herself in coloured garments. Until Rabbi Akiva came and taught: If so, you make her repulsive to her husband, and her husband will end up divorcing her. Rather, what does the verse ‘and she who is ill in her impurity’ teach? She remains in her impurity (the prohibition of closeness applies to her) until she enters the water.” That is, if the woman does not look attractive, there is a concern that her husband will become distant from her and not long for her, and in rare cases they may even come to divorce. Therefore, a woman should not refrain from adorning herself as she needs.

That is, the couple must follow the middle path during the days of prohibition: on the one hand, they should be careful not to arouse the desire between them; on the other, they should be careful not to exaggerate in distancing themselves from each other. Likewise we learned (above 1:4) that one of the reasons for the days of prohibition is to renew longing and love: “The Torah said: let her be impure for seven days, so that she will be as beloved to her husband as at the time she entered the ḥuppa” (Nidda 31b). If during the days of prohibition the wife becomes unattractive to her husband or the husband becomes unattractive to his wife, or they feel too great a distance from each other, they will not merit the renewal of love when they become permitted again. Therefore a woman is permitted to adorn herself during the days of her niddut, while taking care that this not arouse their desire and lead them to transgression (SA 195:9; Torat Ha-shelamim 11). Similarly, it is right that during these days they speak with each other in friendship and compliment each other, in order to preserve the faithful love between them; but they should not converse at length in a way that is liable to arouse their desire.

The principle is understood, but the way to apply it is complex, for on the one hand any expression of friendship and love is also liable to arouse desire, while on the other hand avoiding expressions of friendship and love is liable to cause pain and hurt. Some suggest doing tiring tasks during these days, such as cleaning and maintenance work, or catching up on tasks for work and studies, so that the thirst for connection lessens. This time can also be used for family visits, such as Shabbat with the parents. It is worth noting that among many couples the men want to avoid expressions of closeness, out of concern that their desire will grow stronger and the pain of the distance will be too hard for them; whereas the women want expressions of friendship in order to feel that even during these days they are still loved. Therefore each couple bears the responsibility to pave for itself the middle path that suits it, with the halakha marking the boundaries, both in the safeguards meant to prevent excessive closeness and in the caution against causing pain to one's spouse.2

sections.title: Looking and Singing
sections.html:
During the days of prohibition a husband is permitted to look at his wife and her clothes and to enjoy her beauty, but he should be careful that his heart not be drawn to thoughts of desire belonging to the mitzva of ona (SA 195:7; EH 21:4).

Likewise, during the days of prohibition the husband must be careful not to look at the covered parts of his wife's body, and the wife should cover them in front of her husband during these days.

Some are lenient and hold that the prohibition is to look at the parts of the body that the woman usually covers when she goes about her home during her days of purity. Others are stringent and hold that she must be careful to cover at home in front of her husband also what she usually covers when she goes out of her home, including her hair. In practice, since this safeguard is rabbinic, the halakha follows the lenient view. However, since the value of modesty is great and precious, and through it faithful love is intensified, ab initio it is good to be stringent. Women who are particularly meticulous even cover their hair when they go to sleep, although they are not particular to fasten the head covering in a way that it will not fall off during sleep.3

When a woman is accustomed to sing, she is permitted to sing as usual during the days of prohibition as well, including the Shabbat songs (zemirot). Some are stringent and hold that just as a woman should not sing in front of strangers, so during the days of prohibition she should not sing in front of her husband. The main halakhic view follows the lenient opinion.4

sections.title: Safeguards Regarding Sleeping
sections.html:
During the days of prohibition the couple are forbidden to lie in one bed even if both are clothed and do not touch each other. It is also forbidden to sleep in two separate beds if they touch each other. But if there is some gap between the two beds, it is permitted according to the letter of the law. When possible, it is good to have a gap of about half a metre between the two beds, so that even if they stretch out their arms in their sleep they will not touch each other (SA and Rema 195:6; Darkhei Tahara 5:59).

Among the safeguards: the husband should not lie in his wife's bed, nor the wife in her husband's bed. Likewise they should not use a blanket or pillow designated for the spouse, for these too are considered part of his or her bed. However, if it is a bed, blanket or pillow not designated for either of them, it is permitted.5

A wife should not spread the bedding of her husband's bed in his presence in preparation for sleep, and likewise a husband should not spread the bedding of his wife's bed in her presence in preparation for sleep, since spreading the bedding is a personal act of affection. But not in the spouse's presence it is permitted (Ketubot 61a; SA 195:11). However, when it is not in preparation for sleep, it is permitted to make the spouse's bed even when he or she sees, since in this way it is one of the household chores and not a personal act of affection (Ritva, Ketubot 4b).6

sections.title: Eating Together
sections.html:
Since a meal has great power to draw hearts closer, the Sages set safeguards at meals, so that the couple will remember that they are in the days of prohibition. They should not sit and eat at one table without something to remind them of the prohibition; for example, they may place on the table some item that they do not intend to use during the meal, and both know that it was placed there to remind them of the prohibition. Likewise, if they usually eat on one tablecloth, they can remind themselves of the prohibition by eating on separate tablecloths. They can also agree between themselves that during the days of prohibition they will always use a certain different utensil, or that one of them will change his or her usual place at the table (SA 195:3; Perisha and Taz 1).

If another person eats with them, even a member of the household, or when they eat in a restaurant, they need not place anything to remind them of the prohibition, since it is accepted to behave with restraint in front of other people (Mahariksh; Pitḥei Teshuva 195:5).

They should likewise be careful not to eat together from one bowl. It is not only soup and cooked dishes that they are forbidden to eat from one bowl; even if there was a bowl of hummus between them, they should not dip their bread in it, but each of them should take some of the hummus onto his or her own plate and eat it that way. It is likewise permitted for each of them to spread a spread from one container onto his or her own slice. If there was a bowl of almonds between them, they should not eat directly from it, but each of them should take a few almonds, place them in front of himself or herself, and eat from them (Rambam; Shakh 195:4; Taz 2). If another person eats with them from the same bowl, it is permitted (Masat Binyamin 112).7

Likewise, a husband is forbidden to eat from the leftovers of food or drink that his wife left on her plate or in her cup, because this involves an expression of closeness and affection. Although some Rishonim were lenient in this, in practice one should be stringent, and only in case of need may one rely on the lenient authorities. There are situations in which even the stringent authorities agree to be lenient ab initio, for example where the food or drink was transferred to another vessel, for in this way the expression of closeness is reduced. Likewise, when the wife is not present, the husband is permitted to eat and drink from her leftovers, since he is not thereby showing her closeness. Likewise, if the husband wants to eat leftover food or drink leftover drink and does not know that they are his wife's leftovers, she need not tell him, for only when he knows that he is eating from her leftovers is there an expression of closeness in it (SA and Rema 195:3-4).8

sections.title: Pouring Alcohol and Matters of Affection
sections.html:
Among the safeguards of distance: one should not serve the other wine or an alcoholic drink in the way it is usually served during the permitted days. But with a change it is permitted; for example, instead of placing the glass near the spouse, one should place it a little further away. If one of them knows how to mix an alcoholic drink in a flavourful way, since this involves an expression of personal affection, he or she should be careful not to do so for the other in his or her presence (SA 195:10; 13).

When a woman pours and serves an alcoholic drink to several people, she is permitted to place the drink before her husband as before everyone, since this involves no special affection toward him. Likewise, when a man pours an alcoholic drink for several people, he is permitted to place it before his wife as before everyone. Likewise at Kiddush: if they are alone, he should place the cup before his wife a little further away than usual, and if other people are present, he may place it before her as before everyone.9

During the days of prohibition they should not sit on a swing in the manner of lovers, but it is permitted to sit on one bench even when it sways (Beit Yosef). Some say that they also should not sit on one sofa or one bench in an affectionate manner, in a way that the sitting of one moves the other, lest they come to touching or to closeness of mind; and if their child sits between them, it is permitted (Rema 195:5).

When travelling by bus or car, it is permitted to sit on one seat, without touching each other even through their clothes.

sections.title: Passing from Hand to Hand
sections.html:
Among the safeguards of the prohibition: they should not hand anything to each other, lest they touch each other. In addition, this involves a certain closeness of mind; therefore even a large object should not be passed from one to the other or carried together (SA 195:2). Ab initio one should also be stringent not to throw an object from one to the other (Rema). Therefore, when an object needs to be passed, one should place it on a table or bag, and the other should take it from there. If other people are present and they are embarrassed to pass the object in this way, they should postpone passing it to a convenient time.

However, in case of need one may be lenient. For example, when they need to lift a pram onto a bus or to a second floor, and there is no convenient and natural possibility of getting help from another person, they are permitted to lift the pram together. Likewise, when they need to carry a bed from place to place in the house, they are permitted to carry it together. Likewise, to prevent embarrassment, when there is no other solution, it is permitted to pass an object from hand to hand while being careful not to touch each other. For example, when they need to pass a key from hand to hand, and they have no natural way to pass it by placing it on a table or the like, and one of them is very embarrassed to do it in an unnatural way, they are permitted to pass it from hand to hand to prevent embarrassment. Those who are meticulous plan their actions in advance so that they will not need to be lenient in this.

Likewise they should not pass a small baby between them. But when the baby is already older and knows how to stretch out his arms to go from his mother's lap to his father or vice versa, it is permitted to help him across while being careful not to touch each other (Tashbetz; Pitḥei Teshuva 195:3). In case of need, even when the baby is small and there is no easy way to pass him between them by placing him in a pram or elsewhere, it is permitted to pass him between them while being careful not to touch each other. It is right not to kiss the baby when he is in the other's arms.10

sections.title: During Illness
sections.html:
When, during the days of prohibition, the husband is ill and needs help getting up or dressing and the like, if another person is present who can help him, they should ask for that person's help with any assistance that requires touching the patient's body, even through his clothing. It is even preferable that a professional nurse care for him rather than his wife during her prohibition, because the nurse will care for him as a service, whereas the caring touch of his wife also has an aspect of affection. When they have no possibility of getting help from another person, or the possibility of getting help from another person involves payment, the patient's wife is permitted to help him with what is needed; since the main purpose of the touch is for care and not for the pleasure of desire, in case of need one may be lenient. It is preferable that she wear gloves, and if she needs to help him bathe, she should be careful to wear gloves.

If the wife is ill, one should be more stringent, for since the husband is healthy, there is a concern that through his touching his wife his inclination will overpower him and he will come to sin. Therefore, even when the care involves payment, if they can afford it, they should hire a carer to care for the wife during the days of her prohibition. If it is difficult for them to obtain a carer or difficult for them to pay for it, in a pressing situation, for a great need, the husband is permitted to care for his wife. He should wear gloves on his hands, and both should take care that all his care and touch of her be with kindness and compassion and not with the pleasure of desire.

These leniencies were stated for patients whose illness involves no danger to life, for when there is danger to life it is self-evident that every rescue action must be taken, and one who asks a rabbi at such a time whether he is permitted to save his sick wife is like one who sheds blood (Yerushalmi Yoma 8:5). Thus the leniency applies even when there is no danger to life, provided that the illness has weakened the spouse's entire body to the point that he or she needs to lie in bed and greatly needs help.11

When one of the spouses is seriously injured and in a dangerous condition, and needs an encouraging caress from his or her spouse, and this can help his or her recovery; or when one of the spouses has a terminal illness, his or her strength has run out and his or her days are numbered, and an encouraging touch can improve his or her condition, strengthening him or her to live as well as possible for a few more days or hours: since this is a touch that expresses love and closeness without desire, like the touch between brother and sister, mother and son, father and daughter, the healthy spouse is permitted to caress the patient in order to encourage and strengthen him or her. And although in ordinary times this is not to be permitted during the days of prohibition, in a situation of danger to life or in the difficult days of parting, in which the bond becomes deep and without desire, in case of need one should be lenient.12
